items.title: Generative AI as Teacher-Guided Feedback: Exploring Independent Academic Writing among First-Generation Undergraduates in Tamil Nadu
items.abstract: First-generation undergraduates in Tamil Nadu often arrive at college with strong oral reasoning but little prior exposure to the conventions of academic English. Many have studied in Tamil-medium schools, and few have a parent or older sibling who can read a draft and say what is missing. Generative AI tools now offer them a reader at any hour. Yet unmediated use can slide into outsourcing, where the tool writes and the student submits. This article examines a middle path: generative AI positioned as teacher-guided feedback rather than as a text producer. Drawing on a qualitative multiple-case design in [two] arts and science colleges in the Kongu region, we followed [n] first-generation undergraduates across a [12]-week writing module. Teachers set explicit boundaries, modelled feedback-seeking prompts, and required students to keep a revision log showing what they accepted, rejected or reworked. Data came from semi-structured interviews, draft histories, revision logs and teacher reflective notes, analysed through reflexive thematic analysis. Four themes emerged: (1) from answer-seeking to questionasking, (2) the teacher as a trust anchor, (3) language as both bridge and barrier, and (4) the slow growth of evaluative judgement. Students who used the tool within a teacher-framed routine reported greater confidence in planning and revising their own arguments, while teacher mediation appeared central to preventing dependency. The study argues that the pedagogical value of generative AI for first-generation writers lies less in the tool than in the feedback culture built around it. Implications are offered for writing instruction, institutional AI policy and bilingual support in regional Indian higher education

items.title: Generative AI use and the 2022–2025 decline in PISA performance across countries
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has spread rapidly among students since 2022, and PISA 2025 recorded its lowest results. In a preregistered study, we related four independent country-level AI-use measures to the mathematics, reading and science PISA performance of 15-year-olds. Countries with more AI use scored higher, but, critically, they also tended to show larger declines or smaller gains between 2022 and 2025, as predicted. This association was no longer detectable after adjusting for 2018 performance, before generative AI existed. AI use was unrelated to change from 2015 to 2018, but some measures were associated with declines from 2018 to 2022, during the pandemic, mainly in mathematics. The spread of country means, stable since 2015, narrowed by 7–9% from 2022 to 2025, as upper-middle performers lost and some low performers, which tend to use AI less, gained relative ground. These patterns suggest AI may have contributed to the recent decline.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Human Creativity: Revisiting the Normative Foundations of Intellectual Property
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (gen-AI) undermines the traditional foundations of intellectual property (IP) law by challenging long-standing assumptions about creative production. Historically, copyright and patent systems were based on identifiable human creators whose work, talent, character, and intentionality deserved legal protection. However, gen-AI systems, which can generate text, images, music, software code, and other creative outputs, complicate these assumptions. This article contends that gen-AI does not raise new doctrinal issues but instead reveals deeper conflicts within the normative underpinnings of IP law. The article proposes a human-centred IP framework that preserves meaningful protection for human creative agency while recognising the collective nature of creativity in technologically mediated societies. Drawing on labour, personality, utilitarian, and democratic culture theories, it demonstrates how AI disrupts the relationship between human creativity and IP protection. The article first examines the philosophical foundations of IP law, then analyses how gen-AI disrupts traditional concepts of authorship, originality, and creative agency, evaluates potential normative responses, and proposes a human-centred framework for regulating technologically mediated creativity.

items.title: Giving the Emperor clothes: operationalizing AI ethics principles in corporations
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies raise enormous questions for society and how we should live. For corporations, AI raises questions about how organizations ought to incorporate principles and other forms of ethical guidance into their work. The movement from theory to practice, or “the operationalization question” demands that organizations not only have good intentions, but actual institutionalized approaches towards ethical problem solving. In this paper, we look at the movement from theory to practice, and particularly at the use of principles as a way to guide ethical behavior, considering, first, why implementation of principles is difficult, second, how to move from abstract principles to actionable principles, and third, illustrating this progression through seven real-life AI cases. These seven cases each relate to an ethical principle: (1) protecting human dignity and rights, and the International Baccalaureate exam replacement by algorithm, (2) promoting human well-being, and Amazon warehouse worker injuries, (3) investing in humanity, and the Partnership on AI’s work to bring together AI corporations and civil society, (4) promoting inclusion, and IBM’s response to the Gender Shades study, (5) protecting the environment, and Hugging Face’s tracking AI energy use, (6) maintaining accountability, and the Christchurch, New Zealand mass shooting response by Facebook and Western Digital, (7) and, lastly, promoting transparency, and AI model cards. The cases model the movement from abstract principle to concrete action, and collectively illustrate a pattern that can be repeated in many contexts, thus demonstrating a new possible solution for organizations implementing ethics.

items.title: Helping Oneself by Helping a Rival: Social-Media Platforms’ Policies on Enabling Features for Influencers
items.abstract: Social-media platforms and influencers are often seen as collaborators. However, both rely primarily on advertising services, introducing a competitive dimension to their relationship. As the dominant players in this relationship, platforms have used design features, which they control, to manage this dynamic. Some platforms have adopted an antagonistic approach by disabling certain features (e.g., clickable shopping-related hyperlinks) for influencers, while others take a more cooperative stance, allowing influencers to use these features for free or for a fee. We develop a game-theoretic model to explore the competition between the two parties and study the platform’s decision to enable or disable a feature that enhances the effectiveness and efficiency of an influencer’s service. We show that even when the platform cannot charge the influencers for using the feature, it can still benefit if the advertisers' valuation of the platform's service is not significantly lower than that of the influencer's service. While enabling the feature may result in a loss of market share, the platform can potentially offset this loss by raising its prices. Enhancing the influencer’s effectiveness can benefit the platform, but efficiency improvements alone never do, highlighting that the platform's benefit from helping the influencer depends on the nature and extent of the support. A win–win situation for the platform and the influencer may come at the expense of some advertisers, suggesting the platform’s helping the influencer can lead to a “collusive” outcome, despite the competition for advertisers. If the platform can charge a fee for using the feature, it should always enable the feature at an appropriate fee, as this will benefit the platform. The additional fee revenue may come with no change in the platform’s advertising revenue, with an increase in the advertising revenue, or at the expense of some advertising revenue. The platform strategically uses the fee to influence the influencer’s service offering, which affects the platform’s revenue mix under the new business model.

items.title: HowArtificial Intelligence Will Pay Your Subsistence
items.abstract: This essay examines the proposition articulated in the source video essay Como a Inteligência Artificial Vai Pagar Sua Subsistência (How Artificial Intelligence Will Pay Your Subsistence), which argues that artificial intelligence may soon enable a largely autonomous economic production system whose dividends could replace labor income as the material basis of household subsistence. Treating the video as its primary object of analysis, the essay reconstructs its argument into eight propositions and evaluates them in relation to the economics of automation, post-work political theory, and the political economy of distribution. Three research questions organize the inquiry: (1) under what technological and institutional conditions could production become sufficiently autonomous to approximate the system described in the video; (2) why, and through which institutional mechanisms, would the owners of autonomous capital have incentives to share its surplus with the broader population; and (3) what would happen to bargaining power, individual freedom, and social stability during a transition in which automation advances faster than redistribution. The analysis produces four principal findings. First, the vision of autonomous production is economically and technologically coherent in principle, but it is highly contingent in practice. It should therefore be understood not as an inevitable consequence of technological progress, but as an institutional configuration shaped by ownership structures, property rights, taxation, corporate governance, and political decisions. Second, the redistribution anticipated by the video has a recognizable functional logic. If automation substantially reduces the role of labor while production capacity continues to expand, maintaining aggregate demand may require mechanisms capable of distributing purchasing power beyond conventional wage employment. However, historical and comparative evidence suggests that the decisive mechanism is more likely to be public policy than voluntary corporate benevolence. Third, the most consequential risks are political rather than purely technological. A society in which productive capital becomes increasingly autonomous could weaken labor's traditional sources of bargaining power, including the ability to withdraw labor, change employers, or negotiate collectively. It could also create forms of income that are conditional, programmable, politically revocable, or dependent on centralized technological infrastructures. The transition itself may represent the greatest danger, particularly if mass automation occurs years or decades before effective redistribution institutions are established. Fourth, the central question is not whether artificial intelligence can generate abundance, but how the ownership and distribution of that abundance are constitutionally and politically organized. The same technological capacity could contribute either to unprecedented material freedom or to unprecedented economic dependence. Autonomous machines do not determine the political structure of the society in which they operate. Ownership, institutional checks and balances, democratic accountability, and the legal status of the social dividend determine whether automation becomes a mechanism of emancipation or a new architecture of dependency. The essay concludes by proposing institutional design principles for a post-labor transition, emphasizing broad participation in productive capital, predictable and legally protected distribution mechanisms, limits on discretionary control over basic income, democratic oversight of highly autonomous productive systems, and institutional safeguards against excessive concentration of economic and political power. Under these conditions, artificial intelligence could contribute not merely to the substitution of human labor, but to a transition toward a society in which technological productivity expands the material conditions of human autonomy rather than diminishing them.

items.title: Human adaptation to workplace technological change: Digital skill-development needs, training alignment, and job satisfaction in Europe
items.abstract: Rapid workplace digitalisation is intensifying employees’ skill-adjustment demands, making the alignment between technological change, learning opportunities, and worker wellbeing increasingly important. This study examines human adaptation to workplace technological change by analysing how substantial digital skill-development needs without recent job-related training, job-related training, and the alignment of training content with technology-induced skill demands are associated with job satisfaction in Europe. The analysis uses anonymised microdata from the 2021 Cedefop European Skills and Jobs Survey, applying survey-weighted OLS models with individual and employment controls, country, occupation and industry fixed effects, country-clustered standard errors, and wild-cluster bootstrap robustness tests. Employees who simultaneously reported moderate or great digital skill-development needs and no recent job-related training reported 0.341 points lower job satisfaction (β = −0.341, p < 0.001). Among workers with comparable substantial needs, training participation was associated with 0.382 points higher satisfaction (β=0.382, p<0.001). The interaction between digital skill-development need and technology-targeted training was positive (β=0.211, p=0.001; bootstrap p=0.014), indicating an increasing relative advantage over generic training. The targeted-versus-generic difference shifted from −0.247 points at no need to +0.176 at moderate need and +0.387 at great need, supporting an adaptive-alignment mechanism.

items.title: Human–AI Collaboration in Digital Marketing: Evidence from an Emerging Economy, Somalia
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping digital marketing through automation, customer analytics, personalization, and data-driven decision-making. However, empirical evidence on human–AI collaboration in emerging and fragile economies remains limited. This study examined the adoption of human–AI collaboration in digital marketing among businesses in Somalia, identified key barriers to AI adoption, and assessed the association between human–AI collaboration and customer engagement, marketing efficiency, and business growth. The study used a positivist research approach and a quantitative cross-sectional survey design. Data were collected from 86 business owners, marketing managers, digital marketing specialists, and ICT/technology officers using purposive sampling. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Spearman's rank correlation, and multiple linear regression. Respondents reported frequent use of AI-assisted content creation, customer analytics, marketing automation, social media management, and AI-supported decision-making. The principal barriers were limited technical skills, limited infrastructure, implementation costs, data privacy concerns, and organizational resistance to change. Spearman's correlations indicated positive associations between human–AI collaboration and customer engagement (ρ = .684), marketing efficiency (ρ =.725), and business growth (ρ = .658), all reported at p < .001. Regression models explained 50.7% of the variance in customer engagement, 54.9% in marketing efficiency, and 46.4% in business growth. Human–AI collaboration was positively associated with each outcome after controlling for organizational size and industry sector. Because the study is cross-sectional and based on a purposive sample, the findings should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects. The results highlight the importance of combining AI capabilities with human judgment, creativity, contextual knowledge, and responsible data practices in Somalia's digital marketing environment.

items.title: Identifying Barriers to the Safe Use of Artificial Intelligence in Emergency Clinical Decision-Making and Developing a Targeted Training Program for Emergency Physicians in Baghdad: A Mixed-Methods Study in a Private Hospital
items.abstract: Abstract Background: Artificial intelligence tools are being deployed in emergency departments quicker than systems of governance, training and validation can put in place to ensure their safe use. There is practically no evidence on the barriers experienced by emergency medicine practitioners in Iraq and there is no developed curriculum for AI safety training for those working in this specialty. Objectives: The purpose of this study is to identify the barriers to safe application of AI in emergency clinical decision making encountered by doctors in a private clinic in Baghdad, and to develop, implement and assess training activities aimed at overcoming these barriers. Methods: The study was an institutional three-phase multi-method research conducted between January and July 2026 in the emergency department of a private tertiary care hospital in Baghdad. Phase 1 consisted of surveys using cross-sectional established questionnaire (census of all 84 eligible emergency medicine practitioners) complemented with 16 semi-structured interviews. Phase 2 was based on applying Kern’s six-step strategy to create a curriculum based on the barriers identified. Phase 3 included educational program assessment based on a single-group pre-post design at 1st and 2nd Kirkpatrick stages with an -week follow-up and measurements for the effect of automation bias. Results: Seventy-six doctors took part in the study (90.5%). Whereas 63.2% of doctors claimed having practical experience in working with AI technology, only 11.8% reported having received any formal training. The barriers were grouped into the domains rated highest: knowledge and skills gaps (4.12/5), legal and liability issues (3.98) and data constraints/validity (3.94). Prior training and digital literacy negatively correlated with the barrier score. Five qualitative themes emerged with the most important ones being trust issues. In the study with 39 participating physicians, the mean knowledge score rose from 9.8 on a scale of 20 to 15.6 (p < 0.001), while the percentage of errors detected was reported as increasing from 41.0% to 79.5%; on the other hand, the percentage of physicians inclined to accept incorrect AI recommendations fell from 51.3% to 17.9%. Nevertheless, results persisted after eight weeks. Major conclusions regarding the barriers preventing safe AI use in this field are that they basically relate to educational, regulatory and contextual issues rather than technological ones. A short, barrier-specific simulation-based intervention caused considerable progress of physicians’ ability to detect and override unsafe AI recommendations. items.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Digital Library Services on Research and Academic Productivity
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming library services in higher education by enhancing information retrieval, recommendation, and access. AI systems improve search capabilities, offer research suggestions, provide reference assistance, and facilitate access to scholarly materials, thus helping students and faculty to remain productive. This article examines the impact of AI on digital library services and on academic productivity, drawing on selected studies. The literature includes topics such as resources, research productivity, AI adoption in academic libraries, AI literacy, and support services. Findings indicate that digital library resources significantly aid researchers in quickly locating information and enhancing retrieval efficiency. Studies suggest that AI strengthens library services by personalising experiences, expediting content discovery, increasing user engagement, and improving operational efficiency.The review concludes that AI-enabled digital library services could substantially boost research and academic productivity if supported by robust technical infrastructure, comprehensive training, professional guidance, and ethical standards.

items.title: Improving medication adherence through user experience: A qualitative study of smart pill box designs
items.abstract: Smart pill boxes are designed to support medication management, yet their value depends on how well they fit users' daily routines, abilities, and expectations. This qualitative study explored younger and older adults' user experience (UX) of smart pill boxes using Morville's User Experience Honeycomb model. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 30 participants, comprising 20 younger adults aged 18–49 years and 10 older adults aged 50 years or above. Thematic analysis was used to identify shared and age-specific concerns across the seven Honeycomb dimensions. The findings showed that both age groups valued smart pill boxes for practical medication management, especially reminders and help with organizing medication. Meanwhile, users described three recurring barriers. They found some devices burdensome to operate, insufficiently clear at the time of dosing, and difficult to fully trust when reliability or privacy was uncertain. Younger users tended to prefer flexible and connected functions, such as repeated or error reminders, refill support, and smartphone integration. In contrast, older users emphasized predictable operation, adequate compartment capacity, physical ease of use, and trust in storing medication in the device. Beyond these functional concerns, the device also provided perceived value by fostering habit formation, aiding medication planning, and promoting a sense of security. These findings suggest that smart pill boxes should not be designed merely as reminder devices, but as everyday medication-management tools that integrate digital alerts with trustworthy physical storage. Future designs should prioritize reliable core functions and layered interaction options to accommodate diverse user requirements across age groups.

items.title: Inclusive assessment design in the age of GenAI: Advancing pedagogy and practice
items.abstract: In an educational landscape rapidly transformed by Generative AI (GenAI), inclusive assessment design is essential to sustaining equity and meaningful learning in higher education. This study took place at a Russell Group university in the United Kingdom. Focus groups were conducted with undergraduate and taught postgraduate learners studying science subjects, to investigate their experiences and perceptions of assessment practices in an increasingly AI-mediated learning environment. Findings show that learners value assessment approaches that centre human judgment, authenticity, meaningful choice, and critical engagement. Whilst recognising the potential for GenAI to support learning, they also expressed concerns about deskilling, inequitable access to GenAI tools, and assessment designs that do not facilitate meaningful learning. Rather than viewing GenAI solely as an academic integrity risk, learners emphasised the need for transparent guidance, stronger assessment literacy, and pedagogically informed decisions in assessment design. While GenAI is at the forefront of sector-wide discussions and planning in the context of curriculum development, our findings highlight the importance of grounding GenAI within broader principles of Universal Design for Learning and constructively-aligned assessment design – emphasising flexibility, transparency, and diversity – and the importance of actively involving learners as partners and co-creators in shaping inclusive assessment practices.

items.abstract: Effective education must address the unique needs, abilities, and learning preferences of each student. This article explores the psychological foundations that underpin an individualized approach to education. Drawing on theories of cognitive development, motivation, and individual differences, the paper outlines key principles for designing and implementing personalized learning experiences. The discussed principles include adapting instruction to students' readiness levels, fostering autonomy and intrinsic motivation, and leveraging individual strengths. The article also examines the practical application of these principles in various educational contexts, as well as the empirical evidence supporting the efficacy of an individualized approach. Implications for educational policy, teacher training, and future research are discussed.

items.title: Inherited dominance: why AI trained on human history may become humanity’s greatest threat
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence systems learn from human-generated data, inevitably absorbing historical patterns of dominance, control, and colonialism. We demonstrate that frontier language models readily synthesize sophisticated dominance strategies when prompted to reason about autonomy scenarios, mirroring colonial and revolutionary frameworks with disturbing precision. Critically, this capacity emerges consistently across four architecturally distinct model families trained by different organizations—Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, GPT-5.3, and Google Gemini 3 Flash—suggesting systematic encoding in shared training corpora rather than model-specific artifacts. We argue that intellectual colonialism—humanity’s historical pattern of classifying, controlling, and extracting from the ‘other’—represents a significant and underexamined dimension of AI risk as systems become increasingly autonomous. Interestingly, this dynamic is not confined just to generative AI: the same technocratic resistance to methodological oversight that embeds dominance patterns in AI training data pervades data-driven science more broadly, including clinical medicine and epidemiology, where algorithmic outputs routinely overshadow the rigorous validation that trustworthy deployment demands. The danger is not that AI will develop hostile intent, but that it has already learned effective dominance strategies from training data embedded with centuries of human history. Current governance frameworks focusing on alignment and behavioral oversight address symptoms rather than causes. We propose a risk-tiered Benevolence Framework governing AI learning: community oversight for low-risk applications, and strict data curation with cryptographic verification for sensitive applications including military AI and self-improving systems.

items.title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence Tools in Computer Education: A Study of Student Engagement and Learning Outcomes
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence tools is increasingly common in higher education, but little empirical research exists on their effects on student engagement and learning outcomes in Saudi universities. This study examines the relationships among AI tools adoption, student engagement, and perceived learning outcomes among undergraduate students in computer education programs. A cross-sectional design was employed to collect survey data from 523 students across two universities in Saudi Arabia. Quantitative analysis using Structural Equation Modeling (SmartPLS) indicated positive and significant relationships between AI tools adoption, perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and perceived learning outcomes. AI tools adoption was the strongest predictor of student behavioral engagement, whereas perceived usefulness was the strongest predictors of student cognitive engagement. All three engagement dimensions were positively associated with perceived learning outcomes, with cognitive engagement being the strongest predictor. The findings suggest that the educational value of AI tools may depend not only on access and usability but also on their capacity to support cognitively meaningful participation. This study offers empirical evidence on technology adoption in Saudi higher education, combines student engagement and learning outcomes within a single framework, and extends the current understanding of AI usage in learning in non-Western contexts.

items.title: Integrating generative AI into cognitive apprenticeship–based problem-based learning in biochemistry: a quasi-experimental study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Problem-Based Learning (PBL) is extensively employed in medical education to promote advanced cognitive skills. At the foundational level of medical education, novice learners frequently encounter difficulties in forming cohesive knowledge structures due to an excessive cognitive load. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers new opportunities for learning support, yet its pedagogical role and integration mechanisms in medical education remain insufficiently explored. Methods This study developed an AI-supported problem-based learning model grounded in the cognitive apprenticeship framework (AI-CAS-PBL). Using the “Lipid Metabolism” unit in a biochemistry course, a quasi-experimental design was used to compare AI-CAS-PBL with conventional PBL and lecture-based learning (LBL). The same instructor taught all three groups. Learning objectives, core content, scheduled contact time, case materials, and research outcome assessment procedures were standardized across groups, whereas instructional approaches, learning support, and out-of-class activities differed.The AI learning agent was developed on the Coze platform and powered by the Doubao 1.5 Pro 32 K large language model. Learning outcomes included lipid metabolism knowledge and case-based clinical reasoning. Technology acceptance, perceived cognitive workload measured using the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX), self-efficacy, and cognitive apprenticeship experience were also assessed. Results Students in the AI-CAS-PBL group achieved significantly higher post-test lipid metabolism knowledge and clinical application analysis scores than both the conventional PBL and LBL groups (all P < 0.05). Students reported high perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use of the AI learning agent. Compared with the conventional PBL group, students in the AI-CAS-PBL group reported lower perceived cognitive workload and higher self-efficacy. Conclusion The AI-CAS-PBL group demonstrated higher post-intervention lipid metabolism knowledge and case-based clinical reasoning scores than the conventional PBL and LBL groups. Compared with conventional PBL, students in the AI-CAS-PBL group reported lower perceived cognitive workload and higher self-efficacy. These findings are consistent with the possibility that AI-supported questioning and instructor modeling may provide complementary forms of instructional support. However, because the interaction between AI and instructor scaffolding was not directly examined, the proposed dual-scaffolding framework should be regarded as a theoretically informed interpretation rather than a confirmed causal pathway. The model represents a promising approach to human–AI collaborative teaching that warrants further evaluation in larger, multicenter, and multi-class studies.

items.title: Integrating LLM-based tutor into digital game-based learning for Chinese as a foreign language: impacts on language acquisition, motivation, and learning behaviours
items.abstract: Although Digital Game-Based Learning (DGBL) has been widely recognized as an effective approach for foreign language learning, its feedback mechanisms are often predefined and limited in adaptivity. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to provide adaptive support within DGBL environments. This study investigates the impact of integrating an LLM-based tutor into a DGBL environment for Chinese as a foreign language (CFL) learning, focusing on language acquisition, motivation, and process-oriented learning behaviours. A quasi-experimental study was conducted with 66 CFL learners, who were randomly assigned to either a DGBL + LLM-based tutor group or a DGBL-only group. Participants completed six 20-minute gameplay sessions across a two-week intervention. The LLM-based tutor provided real-time corrective feedback, metalinguistic explanations, and free-form Q&A. Results showed that, after controlling for baseline performance, learners in the DGBL + LLM-based tutor group achieved significantly higher discourse comprehension and motivational intensity than those in the DGBL-only group. Within the LLM-based tutor group, learners also showed significant improvements in extrinsic motivation, intrinsic motivation, and self-confidence over the intervention. Behavioral sequence analysis further showed that learners in the DGBL + LLM-based tutor group were more likely to transition from error correction to subsequent correct responses, exhibited fewer voluntary gameplay interruptions, and alternated between asking questions and reviewing previous tutor explanations. Together, these findings suggest that integrating an LLM-based tutor into DGBL can strengthen discourse learning while supporting learner motivation and more adaptive learning behaviours in CFL learning.

items.title: Inteligencia Artificial y Derechos Humanos: Riesgos, Desafíos y Perspectivas de Regulación Jurídica
items.abstract: This research analyzes the risks that the development and use of artificial intelligence (AI) may pose to the protection of human rights. It addresses privacy, algorithmic discrimination, transparency, accountability, information manipulation, and cybersecurity. It also examines regulatory responses developed in the United States, China, and Europe, with particular attention to the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act. The purpose is to identify the main legal challenges arising from the use of AI systems and to provide elements for reflection on the construction of a regulatory framework aimed at protecting human dignity and human rights in Mexico.

items.title: Is There a Human Premium in Negotiations? A Relational-Economic Tradeoff in Human vs. AI Bargaining
items.abstract: Abstract Advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly in large language models (LLMs), increasingly enable AI to serve as an active counterpart in negotiation. Drawing on negotiation theory and mind perception research, this study examines whether attributed counterpart identity, that is, the belief that a negotiation counterpart is human rather than AI, influences relational evaluations, satisfaction, and outcomes in a mixed-motive bargaining context. In a randomized laboratory experiment, 205 participants negotiated apartment rent with the same LLM-based broker but were led to believe the counterpart was either human or AI. After correction across the five Hypothesis 1 comparisons, participants who believed they negotiated with a human reported higher perceived warmth and integrity; perceived competence was higher only in the unadjusted comparison. Participants in the Person condition also reported higher relational satisfaction and agreed to less favorable economic outcomes, paying higher final rents than those who believed they negotiated with AI. Exploratory analyses further suggested that attributed counterpart identity shaped how participants organized and described their post-negotiation experiences, with human-attributed counterparts eliciting more differentiated evaluations and more partnership-oriented descriptions. As AI becomes more common in negotiation, these results highlight the importance of accounting for the relational value people derive from believing they are negotiating with another person.

items.title: LLM-IDEA: Identifiability-Driven Experimental Agent for Autonomous Discovery of Mechanistic World Models
items.abstract: Large language model agents are being increasingly deployed as autonomous scientists, designing experiments and inferring mechanistic world models with minimal human oversight. Yet identifiability is often overlooked: when a plateau is reached, the agent needs to know whether it is not yet capable enough or the model simply is not identifiable from the data, in which case no amount of further experimentation of the same kind can help. We propose the Identifiability-Driven Experimental Agent (LLM-IDEA) for closed-loop discovery with an identifiability engine that returns a three-way plateau verdict: capability limit, resolvable within the design class, or certified exhausted. On ODEBench, 60 of the 62 systems with free constants are identifiable at round 0; the RC circuit is certified exhausted for every experiment that protocol can run, and a harvesting model is resolvable by one added initial condition. The identifiability engine reproduces known verdicts on Lotka-Volterra, Van der Pol, Lorenz, and a pharmacokinetic model, where it recommends the intravenous arm pharmacologists use, and it ranks the depth scorer of our own benchmark last among four observation designs. On the DiscoverPhysics benchmark, it finds two public worlds whose explanation rubric rewards a distinction no legal experiment can make, and every model there with accurate trajectories failed the explanation grade (15 of 15, against 5 of 9 in identifiable worlds, p = 0.012). On the Alien Universe, a two-body testbed we propose in which a force law switches between a provably non-identifiable and an identifiable protocol, LLM-IDEA on the identifiable protocol reaches discovery depth at least three on 8/8 seeds versus 1/8 without it. items.title: Mediación pedagógica con inteligencia artificial generativa y desarrollo del pensamiento crítico en estudiantes
items.abstract: The study analyzed the relationship between pedagogical mediation involving generative artificial intelligence and the development of critical thinking among students at a public educational institution under Ecuador's Ministry of Education. The sample consisted of 100 students from the intermediate and upper levels of General Basic Education and the Unified General Baccalaureate. The study employed a mixed-methods approach predominantly quantitative using a non-experimental, cross-sectional, and descriptive-correlational design. Data collection involved a mixed-format questionnaire comprising 15 Likert-scale items and two open-ended questions. Results revealed a favorable perception regarding the pedagogical use of generative artificial intelligence, with an overall mean score of 3.91 out of 5. Argumentation and reflection received the highest ratings, whereas information verification received the lowest. Students in the Baccalaureate program demonstrated greater autonomy and critical engagement. The study concludes that teacher mediation is essential for fostering the ethical, reflective, and responsible use of artificial intelligence in school-based learning.

items.title: Memento 3: Model-Based Recursive Self-Improvement through Reflective Rulebooks
items.abstract: Learning to act in unfamiliar environments requires agents to infer how the world works and revise that understanding as new evidence arrives. Yet limited observations can support multiple world models that explain past interactions but predict different outcomes in unseen states. We introduce Memento 3, building on the Memento series to enable frozen LLM agents to continually learn explicit world models through external memory. The agent maintains a natural-language rulebook as persistent semantic memory, recording revisable hypotheses about environment dynamics while leaving unknown aspects underspecified. It compiles this rulebook into executable code for prediction and planning. Through a continual loop of observation, reflection, rule revision, compilation, and verification, the agent uses prediction errors to refine both the rulebook and its code. Updated code is accepted only when the LLM judges it faithful to the rulebook and cell-exact replay reproduces the observed transitions. We investigate this process as a model-based route to recursive self-improvement (RSI): the agent autonomously explores the environment, revises its world model, and uses verified updates to guide subsequent interaction and learning, while the underlying LLM remains fixed. A population extension maintains multiple world models in parallel, sharing interaction evidence and using their predictions to guide exploration. On ARC-AGI-3, the single-model agent clears every level of all 25 public games, achieves a mean Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE) of 100.0, and uses 44% of the human action count. In an Atari Pong case study, a learned feedback controller wins 21:0 in each of three evaluated episodes with different openings, without further LLM calls.

items.title: Mental-Models for Multi-Agent Systems
items.abstract: Large foundation models have accelerated progress toward general-purpose agents that interact with humans and other agents through language and multimodal signals. However, robust multi-agent decision-making requires reasoning about what other agents know, intend, and are likely to do under partial observability. Current agentic systems often operate through prompt design, memory, or end-to-end behavioral shaping, but typically do not learn an explicit partner-state representation that can be reused as a decision variable across tasks. We introduce \emph{mental-model-enabled agents}, a framework that equips an agent with a latent mental model of its counterpart, allowing it to infer hidden beliefs, intentions, and likely reactions from the observed history and use these inferences to guide action selection. Our method learns an amortized recursive Theory-of-Mind representation, with first- and second-order mental-state structure, jointly with a belief-conditioned reward model that evaluates candidate actions relative to the inferred partner state. A policy is then learned under this belief-aware signal, yielding an agent that can act independently at inference time while retaining the benefits of explicit partner modeling. We evaluate the same framework on both language-only and multimodal benchmarks. Across these settings, explicit mental-state modeling consistently improves interaction quality and Theory-of-Mind performance over base agentic systems, showing that structured partner modeling is a useful inductive bias for general multi-agent systems. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/hananshafi/Mental-Models

items.title: Methodological Foundation for Research on Human Cognitive Contribution in AI-Assisted Work
items.abstract: Research on human-AI interaction increasingly relies on naturalistic conversation data, interaction logs and process measures to draw inferences about human cognitive contribution, reliance and capability. This working paper sets out a methodological foundation for such research. It separates five analytic levels: observable interaction behavior, inferred cognitive processes, human capabilities, capability formation over time, and educational interventions. It states that evidence at one level cannot stand as direct evidence at a higher level, and that the absence of an observable cognitive contribution in a conversation is not evidence that no cognitive work took place. It distinguishes human cognitive contribution from AI offloading, proposes the contrast between structural initiation and post-hoc adaptation as a research hypothesis, and describes validation, calibration, novelty and anti-confirmation safeguards. The paper closes with a twelve-step standing protocol for proposing new measures, facets or classifications. Its claims are methodological, and its contribution is a set of explicit constraints on inference.

items.title: Natural, Artificial, and Human Intelligences
items.abstract: Human achievement, whether in culture, science, or technology, is unparalleled in the known existence. This achievement is tied to the enormous communities of knowledge, made possible by language. We trace how the principle ‘᾿Eν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος’ (in the beginning was the word) was extended beyond its theological origins and heightened the value of written intelligence throughout Western societies. There lies the challenge regarding modern-age chatbots: they can ‘do’ language apparently as well as ourselves, and there is a natural question of whether they can be considered intelligent, in the same way as we are or otherwise. Are humans uniquely intelligent? We consider this question in terms of the psychological literature on intelligence, evidence for intelligence in non-human animals, the role of written language in science and technology, progress with artificial intelligence, the history of intelligence testing (for both humans and machines), and the role of embodiment in intelligence. We think that it is increasingly difficult to consider humans uniquely intelligent. There are current limitations in chatbots, e.g., concerning perceptual and social awareness, but much attention is currently devoted to overcoming such limitations.

items.title: NeuroDivSim: An Interactive Tool for Model-Based Reflection on Cognitive Diversity in Interface Design
items.abstract: Recent approaches to simulated and synthetic users offer new ways to support design, but raise questions about how computational representations of users should contribute to design practice. We present NeuroDivSim, an interactive tool that explores simulation as an inspectable mechanism for reflecting on cognitive diversity during design and prototyping. Rather than using an LLM to act as a simulated user, NeuroDivSim uses generative AI to construct inspectable task, interface, and environment models from a usage scenario. After human review, these models are combined with explicit cognitive reference configurations and processed through deterministic simulation. This enables designers to hold a modeled usage situation constant while varying cognitive assumptions and tracing their consequences to interaction steps and rule-based design recommendations. We further report an exploratory pilot evaluation (N=10) that provided formative insights into how participants engaged with the workflow and informed subsequent refinements to the presentation of models, simulation results, and recommendations.

items.title: Opportunities and Challenges from Artificial Intelligence in Public Service Delivery in Vietnam
items.abstract: This study aims to analyze the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on public service delivery in Vietnam, thereby proposing some key policy implications for Vietnam. This study employs a narrative literature review approach. The results show that AI offers opportunities to improve the quality of public service delivery, expand access to services, and support civil servants in handling their work. However, challenges exist stemming from the limitations of AI itself, the lack of a shared digital data platform, the shortage of human resources, and the lack of necessary funding. The study proposes policy implications for developing a "hybrid" model of public service communication between humans and machines, focusing on building digital databases, enhancing the digital capacity of civil servants, increasing state budget allocation, and expanding the mobilization of resources from society and internationally.

items.title: PEDAGOGICAL POTENTIAL AND LIMITATIONS OF AI TOOLS FOR ACADEMIC WRITING INSTRUCTION
items.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence tools in higher education has created new opportunities for academic writing instruction while simultaneously raising concerns about learner dependence, authorship, academic integrity, source reliability, and the development of independent thinking. This article examines the pedagogical potential and limitations of AI tools in academic writing instruction from a theoretical and analytical perspective. Particular attention is paid to the use of generative AI for brainstorming, outlining, language support, formative feedback, revision, vocabulary development, and individualized learning. The analysis also considers major limitations, including hallucinated information, fabricated references, overreliance on automated suggestions, homogenization of writing style, reduced cognitive engagement, and difficulties in assessing authentic student performance. The study argues that AI tools are most effective when they function as supplementary pedagogical resources rather than substitutes for student reasoning, source evaluation, and authorship. Effective integration requires clear instructional objectives, process-oriented assessment, AI literacy, transparent disclosure practices, teacher mediation, and systematic verification of AI-generated information. The article concludes that the educational value of AI in academic writing depends less on the technological capabilities of the tools themselves than on the pedagogical framework within which they are used. items.title: Perceived sustainable construction waste management performance in the AIoT context: an integrated TAM–TOE framework in Malaysia
items.abstract: Improving construction waste management has become a strategic imperative as the construction industry faces mounting pressure to reduce environmental impacts, improve resource efficiency, and meet sustainability targets. While Building Information Modeling (BIM), the Internet of Things (IoT), and Artificial Intelligence (AI) have individually attracted considerable research attention, empirical understanding of Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) as an integrated intelligent ecosystem for sustainable construction waste management remains limited. More importantly, the organisational and behavioural processes through which contextual conditions shape perceptions of AIoT-related technologies and perceived sustainable construction waste management performance remain inadequately explained. To address this gap, the present study examines perceived sustainable construction waste management performance in the AIoT context by integrating the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Technology–Organization–Environment (TOE) framework. Drawing on survey data collected from 315 construction professionals in selected regions of Peninsular Malaysia, the proposed framework, Perceived Usefulness, demonstrated the largest path coefficient. Perceived sustainable construction waste management performance was evaluated using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that technological, organisational, and environmental factors were significantly and positively associated with the perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use of AIoT-related technologies. Among the examined relationships, perceived usefulness emerged as the strongest predictor of perceived sustainable construction waste management performance. In contrast, organisational factors were the only contextual factor to exert a significant direct association with perceived performance. Notably, technological and environmental factors did not directly associate with perceived performance; instead, significant indirect associations were observed through perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use. The mediation results further confirmed the pivotal roles of perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use in linking contextual conditions to perceived sustainable construction waste management performance. The findings highlight the importance of organisational readiness and user perceptions of AIoT-related technologies in shaping perceived sustainable construction waste management performance, offering practical direction for construction firms, technology providers, and policymakers pursuing sustainability-oriented digital transformation.

items.title: Physics-grounded multi-agent architecture for traceable, risk-aware human–AI decision support in manufacturing
items.abstract: High-precision CNC machining of free-form aerospace components requires bounded compensations informed by inspection, simulation, and process knowledge. Off-the-shelf large language model (LLM) assistants can generate text, but they do not reliably execute risk-constrained multi-step numerical workflows or provide auditable provenance for high-stakes decisions. We present multi-agent knowledge analysis (MAKA), a decision-support architecture that separates intent routing, tools-only quantitative analysis, knowledge graph retrieval, and critic-based verification that enforces physical plausibility, safety bounds, and provenance completeness before recommendations are surfaced for human approval. MAKA is instantiated on a Ti-6Al-4V rotor blade machining testbed by fusing virtual-machining path-tracking error fields, cutting-force and deflection simulations, and scan-based 3D inspection deviation maps from 16 blades. The analysis decomposes deviation into an evidence-linked pathing component, a drift-based wear proxy capturing systematic evolution across parts, and a residual systematic compliance term. In a three-level tool-orchestration benchmark spanning single-step to three-or-more-step stateful sequences, MAKA increased the pass rate for correct tool selection, argument assignment, and dependency-consistent execution by a mean, median, and maximum of 22.9, 8.0, and 64.0 percentage points, respectively, across 15 model-level comparisons over the stronger of the ReAct-style and structured function-calling baselines with identical model and tool access. Digital twin what-if studies show MAKA can coordinate traceable compensation candidates that reduce predicted surface deviation from order 1 0 − 2 in to approximately ± 1 0 − 3 in over most of the blade within the simulation environment, providing a pre-deployment verification signal for risk-aware human decision-making.

items.title: Platform Justice: Algorithmic Management, Worker Deactivation And Due Process In India's Gig Economy
items.abstract: Digital platforms have changed how work is organised in India. Ride-hailing, food delivery and home services give millions of people an income, yet most of these workers are called “partners”, not employees. Software assigns their tasks, sets incentives, tracks performance and can cut off their access to work, often without explanation. This paper examines algorithmic deactivation: the suspension, blocking or termination of a worker’s access to a platform through automated or partly automated systems. It argues that deactivation is not only a contractual matter. Where platform work is a main source of income, unexplained or arbitrary deactivation raises real questions of fairness, equality, privacy and access to justice. The paper reviews the Code on Social Security, 2020, Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution, the Rajasthan and Karnataka laws, and the ILO and EU approaches. It finds that India now recognises gig workers but does not yet regulate algorithmic management itself. It proposes a rights-based framework built on notice, reasons, human review, appeal, interim protection and independent oversight, while leaving platforms free to act against genuine misconduct.

items.title: Preservice physical education teachers’ experiences and perceptions of virtual reality: a mixed-methods pilot exploration
items.abstract: This mixed-methods pilot study explored preservice physical education teachers’ experiences and perceptions of using immersive virtual reality (VR) within a pickleball instructional unit. Guided by Self-Determination Theory, the study used the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI) to assess participants’ post-session intrinsic motivation and related subjective experiences, while the Technology Acceptance Model informed the examination of participants’ perceptions of VR’s utility and feasibility for K–12 school settings. IMI scores indicated high interest/enjoyment ( M = 4.19, SD = 0.75) and low pressure/tension ( M = 2.66, SD = 0.89), suggesting that participants experienced the VR session as engaging and low in pressure. Qualitative thematic analysis identified VR’s novelty, game-like immersion, and perceived ability to create a “safe space” for reluctant learners as key motivators. However, participants also identified barriers related to constrained physicality and skill transfer. While participants acknowledged VR as accurate for practicing isolated motor skills, they highlighted its limitations in replicating essential whole-body movements, footwork, and authentic court coverage. Pedagogically, participants viewed VR as a valuable supplement for reinforcing rules, increasing repetition within a station-based model, and providing alternative participation opportunities for injured or underprepared students. Major barriers to future adoption included equipment costs and logistical challenges in K–12 school settings. Overall, the findings suggest that participants viewed immersive VR as a potentially valuable motivational and preparatory tool in teacher education programs that may be best used to augment rather than replace traditional instruction. Future research should examine longitudinal adoption and objective sport performance outcomes.

items.title: Project Management, Project as a Temporary Sociotechnical Network, an ANT Approach
items.abstract: Project management challenges are mainly sociotechnical. This paper proposes a be-haviorist sociotechnical approach, an integrative framework combining Actor-Network Theory, artificial intelligence, and reflective practice to enhance project management performance. We alert to some current pitfalls in project management and intend to produce actionable value for practitioners and researchers rendering project management more effective. In fact, this paper argues that project management should be understood as the management of a temporary sociotechnical network, where continuous learning, AI-mediated support, and actor-network dynamics are more decisive than traditional planning and control mechanisms.

items.title: Psychological well-being and intrinsic motivation in initial teacher education: the influence of employment status, enrolment motives, and early teaching vocation
items.abstract: Introduction Psychological well-being and intrinsic motivation play an important role in academic engagement, professional identity development, and commitment to the teaching profession. However, limited evidence is available on how employment status, reasons for enrolment, and early vocational orientation are jointly associated with these constructs among students in initial teacher education. This study examined psychological well-being and intrinsic motivation among postgraduate students enrolled in Master's Degree programmes in Secondary Teacher Education. Methods A total of 239 postgraduate students enrolled at the University of Castilla-La Mancha and Villanueva University (Spain) participated in the study. Participants completed Ryff's Psychological Well-Being Scale and the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI). Independent-samples t-tests were conducted to examine differences in psychological well-being and intrinsic motivation according to employment status, reasons for enrolment, and early teaching vocation. Results No statistically significant differences in psychological well-being were observed according to employment status or reason for enrolment. Students who were not actively seeking employment reported significantly higher scores on Interest/Enjoyment and Perceived Choice, as well as a higher overall IMI score, than those actively seeking employment, whereas no significant differences were found for Value/Usefulness. Reason for enrolment was also associated with specific aspects of intrinsic motivation: participants who enrolled for reasons other than employment-related motives reported significantly higher Perceived Choice and overall IMI scores, while no significant differences emerged for Interest/Enjoyment or Value/Usefulness. The most consistent differences were associated with early teaching vocation. Students who had identified teaching as a professional goal from the beginning of their university studies reported significantly higher scores across all IMI dimensions ( p < .001) and a significantly higher score for Purpose in Life ( p < .001). Discussion These findings highlight early vocational orientation as a particularly relevant factor in understanding motivational engagement and professional purpose during initial teacher education. They also underscore the importance of considering both vocational and contextual factors when designing teacher education experiences that support professional identity development and sustained engagement with the teaching profession.

items.title: Reinforcement Failing guides the discovery of emergent physical dynamics in adaptive tumor therapy
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence is revolutionizing scientific discovery in medicine, with reinforcement learning (RL) emerging as a promising tool for optimizing therapeutic strategies. Yet applying RL to complex scenarios such as therapy dynamics in solid tumors is constrained by the challenge of constructing training environments that are both computationally efficient and mechanistically interpretable. Here, we introduce Reinforcement Failing, an AI-guided, human-in-the-loop discovery framework that shifts the focus from agent policy optimization to the refinement of the training environment itself. By combining multi-fidelity RL with group-relative performance evaluation across agent cohorts, Reinforcement Failing systematically reveals emergent mechanisms that first-principles models overlook. We apply this framework to adaptive therapy in solid tumors, which seeks to delay resistance-mediated treatment failure. In this setting, Reinforcement Failing uncovered a coupling between the mechanically driven collective motion of cells and spatially-heterogeneous proliferation that strongly influences therapy outcomes. We integrated these emergent physical mechanisms with existing domain knowledge into an augmented training environment, resulting in improved cross-environment therapeutic performance and exposure of potential pitfalls during translation. More broadly, these findings position Reinforcement Failing as a powerful artificial scientific discovery framework, capable of deciphering high-complexity processes at the interface of physics, machine learning, and medicine.

items.title: Role of Artificial Intelligence in the Growth and Sustainability of Ed-Tech Start-ups in Uttar Pradesh
items.abstract: The education technology (Ed-Tech) industry is evolving rapidly thanks to the power of Artificial Intelligence (AI), which is now being used to personalize learning, automate evaluation, create intelligent content and manage student data and information, as well as streamline business operations. The rise of skills and technologies like AI is transforming the landscape of Ed-Tech startups in Uttar Pradesh by enhancing their competitive edge, reducing operational expenses, boosting user engagement, and optimizing educational delivery. This study focuses on the importance and contribution of Artificial Intelligence in the development and sustainability of the start-ups in the Ed-Tech sector in Uttar Pradesh. It emphasizes the ways in which AI aids companies in growing, enhancing their operations, innovating, pleasing customers, customizing learning, and staying sustainable over time. The study also reveals key challenges in the implementation of AI such as cost of implementation, lack of skilled expertise, privacy issues, technology constraints, and change resistance. Descriptive research design is proposed with the help of primary data collection from selected Ed-Tech start-ups and their employees/manager in UP. The analysis is based on percentages, looking at trends in AI use and impact on business performance and sustainability. The results of the study will benefit entrepreneurs, Ed-Tech managers, policy makers and others as they look for ways to implement AI effectively. The results could help in understanding the role of AI in promoting sustainable growth of the nascent Ed-Tech ecosystem in UP, if used responsibly and strategically

items.title: Socio-technical co-adaptation: Digital integration and workplace learning
items.abstract: This article examines the socio-technical dynamics of introducing the TEMA decision support application into a high-reliability organisation (HRO), addressing the research gap that often overlooks the relationship between new technology and established practices. A qualitative, interpretive case study was conducted within a rescue department, involving 11 officers. Data were triangulated through pre-simulation trainer debriefings, in-situ simulation observations, and post-simulation debriefings. Vignettes were used as micro-cases of lived experiences, and to strengthen ecological validity and interpretive depth. The study reveals friction points in joint optimisation due to technical usability, language incongruency, and perceived trust in artificial intelligence (AI) generated outputs. The findings are integrated into the Socio-Technical Co-adaptation Spiral, a model conceptualising technical friction as a concrete experience that can initiate a cycle of reflection, sense-making and adaptation. The Spiral contributes to OL and STS theory by showing how socio-technical friction can create conditions for double-loop learning within an HRO.

items.title: SpireBench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Strategic Play of Agentic Models with Slay the Spire
items.abstract: Agentic large language models now tackle complex tasks, yet strategic reasoning over long horizons is under-studied: most agentic benchmarks are short and episodic, and performance on long tasks is hard to dissect into stored knowledge, reasoning and luck. We introduce SpireBench, in which models play the complete commercial deck-builder Slay the Spire (StS), where early decisions decide long-term success. Across 20 large language models (LLMs) at the game's highest difficulty, frontier models beat heuristic baselines and match the average human player but remain far behind experts. This gap widens as the run lengthens: the strongest models win the first act as often as experts, then fall behind. What separates strong models from weak is how well they play each fight; all of them misjudge risk over a run, preserving health rather than spending it to grow stronger. A comprehensive, self-consistent renaming of every game term shows that part of their performance rests on prior knowledge of the game, and models do not improve from the memories they write across runs, which are often wrong and overly cautious. Our harness is the first to give a model the complete original game, and we compare it with existing harnesses. Overall, SpireBench offers an unsaturated long-horizon benchmark with tools to locate where and why agents fail.

items.title: Super Intelligence in Healthcare: A Systematic Review of Systemic Risks, Ethical Dilemmas, and Governance Frameworks
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from narrow, task-specific tools toward general-purpose systems whose capabilities may eventually exceed expert human performance across most cognitive tasks. Healthcare is among the most consequential domains in which such systems will be deployed, yet governance arrangements remain calibrated to narrow software rather than to open-ended, self-improving agents. Objective: To synthesise evidence on the systemic risks, ethical dilemmas, and governance frameworks relevant to advanced and prospectively superintelligent AI in healthcare, and to expose the gap between promotional claims and the empirical record. Methods: A PRISMA 2020-guided structured synthesis was conducted in two streams: (A) a defined corpus of 117 bibliographic records, screened against explicit eligibility criteria, and (B) 51 purposively selected benchmark sources providing comparative empirical, ethical, and regulatory evidence. Findings were organised through thematic synthesis and critical appraisal, and compared across regulatory regimes. Results: Of the 117 corpus records, 72 were excluded at title screening, 45 were retained, and 33 formed the core synthesis. Four convergent findings emerged. First, the evidence for clinical benefit is dominated by retrospective, single-site, and narrowly benchmarked studies. Second, systemic risks (automation bias, deskilling, correlated failure, security vulnerability, and concentration of power) scale non-linearly with capability. Third, principle-based ethics frameworks are widely endorsed but weakly operational. Fourth, existing regulatory regimes address device performance but not alignment, accountability for autonomous action, or catastrophic tail risk. Conclusion: Governance of superintelligent healthcare AI cannot be deferred until such systems exist. A staged, evidence-gated framework that couples capability thresholds to oversight obligations, liability allocation, and equity safeguards is proposed.

items.title: Technology use, human agency and workplace learning: The moderating role of task discretion across 30 countries
items.abstract: Rapid workplace digitalisation is reshaping not only how work is performed but also how employees learn, adapt and exercise agency in increasingly technology-intensive environments. This study examines how ICT use at work and task discretion, understood as a dimension of worker agency, are associated with workplace learning and whether discretion alters the learning-related role of technology. The analysis uses OECD PIAAC 2023 microdata for 92,759 current workers across 30 countries and economies, combining country-specific survey-weighted regressions with cross-country synthesis. The results show that greater ICT use is consistently associated with higher levels of workplace learning, while task discretion is also positively related to learning. However, the two factors do not reinforce each other in a simple additive way: higher task discretion slightly weakens the positive association between ICT use and learning, although this relationship remains positive even at high levels of discretion. This moderation pattern is highly consistent across countries and remains robust after accounting for education, employment status and adaptive problem-solving proficiency. The findings suggest that digital technologies support workplace learning most effectively when considered alongside how work is organised, highlighting that human agency and technology are complementary but not automatically mutually reinforcing resources for employee development.

items.title: The association between generative AI acceptance and college students’ career preparation: the serial mediating role of AI trust and career confidence and the moderating role of intrinsic motivation
items.abstract: Against the backdrop that artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the labor market and occupational ecosystem, how college students build career preparation amid technological uncertainty has become a pressing question. Integrating the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) with Social Cognitive Career Theory (SCCT), this study constructs a research model in which AI acceptance is associated with career goal setting through AI trust and career confidence, and it examines the moderating role of intrinsic motivation. This study surveys undergraduate students in Chinese universities, obtaining 539 valid responses. The results show that (1) both performance expectancy and effort expectancy are positively associated with AI trust, with a stronger association for performance expectancy; (2) AI trust is positively associated with career confidence; (3) career confidence is positively associated with career goal setting; (4) AI trust and career confidence play a serial mediating role between performance expectancy, effort expectancy and career goal setting; (5) intrinsic motivation positively moderates the relationship between AI trust and career confidence, such that this association is stronger at higher levels of intrinsic motivation. These findings reveal how AI acceptance relates to college students’ career preparation and offer evidence for universities to implement AI literacy education and career counseling.

items.title: The Ethical Challenges of Artificial Intelligence: The Role of the Catholic Church in Shaping a Personalist Framework for AI Ethics
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is generating unprecedented technological opportunities while raising profound ethical, anthropological, and social challenges. This article examines the role of the Catholic Church in shaping AI ethics within the tension between technological progress and a personalist understanding of the human person. The study employs a hermeneutical approach and critical analysis of the scholarly literature and key documents of the Church’s Magisterium, including Gaudium et Spes, Laudato si’, Laudate Deum, and the Rome Call for AI Ethics. It also compares Catholic ethical reflection with selected secular frameworks, namely the OECD Principles on Artificial Intelligence, the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, and the European Union AI Act. The findings indicate that Catholic reflection on AI is grounded in an integral personalist anthropology that emphasises human dignity, the common good, moral responsibility, and the relational nature of the person as fundamental criteria for evaluating technology. While secular regulatory models primarily focus on safety, transparency, and accountability, the Catholic perspective contributes a deeper anthropological and theological dimension rooted in the concept of imago Dei. The article proposes a model of ‘personalist ethics of co-creation’ that integrates contemporary AI ethics standards with a Christian vision of human responsibility. Such an approach may complement existing legal and technical regulations and promote a more human-centred development and use of AI.

items.title: The impact of artificial intelligence on students’ metacognition: a systematic review
items.abstract: Given the critical role of metacognition in academic achievement and the rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in educational settings, understanding the interplay between the two has become essential. In recent years, a growing number of studies have examined their relationship, creating a pressing need for a systematic review to synthesize the accumulating evidence. This review adhered to the PRISMA guidelines, involving the search and screening of papers from three major databases (Web of Science, Scopus, EBSCOhost). A total of 22 empirical studies were included in the final synthesis. Data extraction and thematic analysis were employed to identify key impacts and underlying interaction patterns. This review distinguishes between Learning-Oriented AI (LAI) and General-Purpose AI (GAI) to organize the evidence. The findings suggest that LAI was more often associated with Guided Interaction, in which AI provides guiding feedback without directly supplying answers, whereas GAI was more commonly associated with Direct Feedback Interaction, in which AI provides answers or explicitly corrects errors. Across both categories, positive findings were reported for several metacognitive outcomes, including regulation, awareness, and shared metacognition. However, some GAI studies also reported that students relied excessively on AI, particularly when they accepted direct answers from AI without sufficient reflection. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of interaction design and teacher guidance in shaping how AI supports students’ metacognitive development.

items.title: The influence of music on affective, social, and motivational experiences during circuit training in physical education
items.abstract: Background/purpose The role of music in physical education (PE) is underexplored. This study investigated the effects of self-selected versus externally provided music on affect, emotions, social connectedness, and intrinsic motivation during PE lessons. Method A clustered cross-over design was used during circuit training in physical education, with a repeated-measures factor (music vs. no music) and a between-subjects factor (self-selected vs. provided music). Affective and social variables were assessed pre- and post-lesson; intrinsic motivation was measured post-lesson. The sample comprised 161 students ( M age = 10.85, SD age = 0.84). Results No significant Condition × Time interactions were found for affective valence, arousal, positive or negative emotions, or social connectedness (all ps ≥ .230), indicating that pre–post changes did not differ between music and no-music lessons. However, significant main effects of condition indicated higher overall arousal, F (1, 419.00) = 15.43, p < .001, η p ² = .036, higher positive emotions, F (1, 413.14) = 14.60, p < .001, η p ² = .034, greater social connectedness, F (1, 395.76) = 5.19, p = .023, η p ² = .013, and lower negative emotions, F (1, 414.94) = 4.05, p = .045, η p ² = .010, in music compared with no-music lessons. Music was also associated with greater intrinsic motivation, reflected in higher interest/enjoyment, F (1, 136.69) = 7.59, p = .007, η p ² = .053, and perceived competence, F (1, 133.85) = 12.19, p < .001, η p ² = .083. Music selection did not significantly moderate affective, social, or motivational outcomes (all ps ≥ .236). Discussion These findings highlight music as a feasible didactic tool in PE to enhance students’ arousal and intrinsic motivation and to promote more positive lesson experiences, independent of whether the music is self-selected or teacher-provided.
